blocks.text: An electroencephalograph (EEG) is a medical instrument that records the electrical activity of the brain through electrodes placed on the scalp.
The resulting recording is called an electroencephalogram.

EEG detects voltage fluctuations produced mainly by the synchronized activity of populations of cortical neurons. It is particularly useful in the evaluation of seizures, epilepsy, altered consciousness, and selected encephalopathies.

items.text: Category: Neurological diagnostic equipment.
Type: Non-invasive neurophysiological recording instrument.
Function: Records cerebral electrical activity.
Recording method: Scalp electrodes connected to an amplifier and computer.
Output: EEG waveforms displayed and stored for interpretation.

blocks.title: A conventional EEG system commonly includes:

items.text: Multiple scalp electrodes.
Electrode caps or individual electrode holders.
Conductive paste or gel, depending on the system.
Lead wires.
Signal amplifiers.
A computer and display.
Recording and analysis software.
An electrode impedance-testing function.

blocks.text: Modern systems may be digital and portable, and some use wireless or ambulatory recording.

"This is an electroencephalograph, a non-invasive neurological diagnostic instrument used to record the electrical activity of the brain through scalp electrodes. It is commonly used to investigate epilepsy and seizures, assess selected causes of altered consciousness, and detect characteristic patterns of cerebral dysfunction."
Examiner tip: EEG records electrical activity; it does not directly measure cerebral blood flow or structural brain anatomy.

content_groups.group_title: A. Investigation of seizures and epilepsy

items.text: Support the diagnosis of epilepsy.
Identify epileptiform discharges.
Classify seizure types and epilepsy syndromes in the appropriate clinical context.
Assess the risk of seizure recurrence in selected situations.
Support presurgical evaluation for drug-resistant epilepsy.

blocks.text: Important: A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy.

blocks.title: EEG may be used to investigate:

items.text: Unexplained episodes of altered awareness.
Suspected non-convulsive status epilepticus.
Persistent impaired consciousness after a convulsive seizure.
Selected cases of unexplained coma or encephalopathy.

blocks.text: Continuous EEG monitoring is particularly valuable when ongoing seizure activity is suspected but cannot be identified reliably from clinical observation alone.
EEG may demonstrate generalized slowing or other patterns associated with cerebral dysfunction due to metabolic, toxic, infectious, or structural causes.
However, EEG findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical assessment and other investigations.

blocks.title: Continuous EEG may be used in selected critically ill patients to:

items.text: Detect non-convulsive seizures.
Monitor seizure treatment.
Evaluate unexplained fluctuations in consciousness.
Support assessment of cerebral electrical activity after severe brain injury.
Sleep-related neurological investigations.
Evaluation of selected paroxysmal events.
Presurgical assessment in epilepsy.
Brain death/death by neurological criteria assessment as an ancillary investigation in selected circumstances, where permitted by applicable protocols.

blocks.text: EEG alone cannot establish brain death. Clinical criteria and applicable legal and institutional requirements must be satisfied.

blocks.text: The internationally used 10–20 system is a standardized method for positioning scalp electrodes.
The numbers refer approximately to electrode spacing as percentages of measured head distances, rather than to the number of electrodes.

items.text: Fp: Frontopolar.
F: Frontal.
C: Central.
T: Temporal.
P: Parietal.
O: Occipital.

blocks.text: Letters indicate approximate scalp regions. Odd-numbered electrodes generally refer to the left hemisphere, even-numbered electrodes to the right, and z indicates the midline.
Examples include Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, C3, C4, P3, P4, O1, and O2.

items.text: Routine EEG: A short recording, often around 20–30 minutes of recording time, with duration varying by protocol.
Sleep-deprived EEG: Uses sleep deprivation to increase the chance of detecting epileptiform abnormalities in selected patients.
Sleep EEG: Records cerebral activity during sleep.
Ambulatory EEG: Records over an extended period while the patient carries a portable recorder.
Continuous EEG: Prolonged monitoring, commonly in critically ill patients.
Non-invasive: Routine scalp EEG does not require surgical access to the brain.
Excellent temporal resolution: Captures rapid changes in cerebral electrical activity.
Useful in epilepsy: Can demonstrate epileptiform discharges that support diagnosis and classification.
Detects non-convulsive seizures: Particularly useful during continuous monitoring in selected patients.
Portable options: Ambulatory systems allow prolonged recording outside the hospital.
Relatively accessible: Routine EEG is generally less expensive than many advanced neuroimaging investigations.
Supports treatment monitoring: Can assess changes in cerebral electrical activity during selected treatments.
Limited spatial resolution: It is less precise than structural imaging for locating many brain lesions.
Artifacts: Eye movements, muscle activity, sweating, and movement can distort the recording.
Normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy: Abnormal activity may not occur during the recording.
Interpretation requires expertise: Waveforms must be interpreted by appropriately trained clinicians.
Scalp recordings may miss deep activity: Some seizures originating in deep brain structures may not produce clear scalp EEG abnormalities.
Recording duration matters: A brief routine EEG may miss intermittent events.
Patient cooperation may be necessary: Movement and poor electrode contact can reduce recording quality.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to Use It — Step-by-Step OSCE Demonstration

blocks.text: Explain that the procedure records the brain's electrical activity using electrodes placed on the scalp.
Reassure the patient that routine EEG is generally painless.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Confirm identity and obtain consent

blocks.text: Check the patient's details and explain the procedure, duration, and any activation procedures planned.
Position the patient comfortably, usually sitting or lying down.
Inspect the scalp and prepare the hair and skin according to the laboratory protocol.
Use the standardized 10–20 system to identify the correct electrode positions.
Apply the appropriate electrodes using conductive paste, gel, or a cap.
Ensure secure attachment and acceptable electrode impedance.
Connect the electrodes to the amplifier and computer.
Confirm that the channels are displaying usable signals without excessive artifact.
Ask the patient to relax and remain still.

items.text: Eyes open.

content_groups.group_title: Step 8: Perform activation procedures when indicated

items.text: Intermittent photic stimulation.
Hyperventilation.
Sleep recording.

blocks.text: Activation procedures are not mandatory for every patient and must be selected according to clinical indications and safety considerations.
Observe for clinical events, unusual movements, changes in awareness, or a suspected seizure.
Document relevant events and their timing.
Remove electrodes carefully, clean the scalp as needed, and ensure that the recording is saved with the appropriate patient details.
The EEG should be reviewed by a qualified clinician, taking into account the patient's history, examination, and reason for the investigation.

"I would ensure that the electrodes are correctly positioned, the signal quality is adequate, and the patient is comfortable throughout the procedure. I would document any clinical events and arrange for the EEG recording to be interpreted by an appropriately trained clinician."

blocks.text: Important: EEG electrodes record electrical activity; they do not ordinarily deliver electrical stimulation to the brain.
EEG rhythms are described by their frequency, amplitude, distribution, and relationship to the patient's state of wakefulness or sleep.

blocks.text: Spike: A brief, sharply contoured transient that may have epileptiform significance.
Sharp wave: A transient with a longer duration than a typical spike.
Epileptiform discharge: An EEG pattern associated with increased propensity for seizures, interpreted in context.
Electrographic seizure: An EEG event meeting accepted criteria for seizure activity, which may or may not have obvious clinical manifestations.
An EEG may show focal or generalized epileptiform abnormalities, depending on the epilepsy syndrome.

items.text: A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy.
An epileptiform discharge does not automatically prove that every reported episode is epileptic.
EEG findings must be correlated with the clinical history and observed events.

blocks.text: Diffuse slowing may occur in metabolic, toxic, infectious, or other forms of cerebral dysfunction.
EEG can support the assessment of encephalopathy, but it does not usually identify the exact underlying cause by itself.
EEG is particularly important in pediatric neurology because seizures, epilepsy syndromes, and normal EEG patterns vary with age.

blocks.text: Hypsarrhythmia is a markedly disorganized EEG pattern classically associated with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome.
It consists of high-amplitude, irregular, disorganized slow waves with multifocal epileptiform discharges. The pattern may vary with sleep and age.
OSCE pearl: Suspected infantile epileptic spasms require urgent pediatric neurological assessment; EEG is an important part of the evaluation but should not delay clinical referral.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE Questions and Model Answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is an EEG?
An electroencephalogram is a recording of the brain's electrical activity obtained using electrodes, usually placed on the scalp.
Q2. What is the difference between an electroencephalograph and an electroencephalogram?
The electroencephalograph is the recording instrument; the electroencephalogram is the resulting tracing or record.
Q3. What is the 10–20 system?
A standardized method of positioning scalp EEG electrodes based on measured head distances, with positions corresponding approximately to 10% or 20% intervals.
Q4. What is the main indication for EEG?
Evaluation of suspected seizures and epilepsy, although EEG has other neurological applications.
Q5. What is the normal adult alpha rhythm?
Approximately 8–13 Hz, typically prominent over posterior regions during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed.
Q6. Does a normal EEG exclude epilepsy?
No. Epileptiform activity may not occur during a routine recording, so clinical assessment and additional testing may still be required.
Q7. What is the difference between EEG and EMG?
EEG records cerebral electrical activity, whereas EMG assesses the electrical activity of skeletal muscles.
Q8. What is an epileptiform discharge?
An EEG pattern, such as a spike or sharp wave, associated with an increased propensity for seizures when interpreted in the appropriate clinical context.
Q9. What is the role of continuous EEG?
It is used in selected patients to detect ongoing seizures, including non-convulsive seizures, and to monitor cerebral electrical activity over prolonged periods.
Q10. What is hypsarrhythmia?
A markedly disorganized, high-amplitude EEG pattern associated classically with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome.
Q11. What are common causes of EEG artifacts?
Eye movements, blinking, muscle activity, movement, poor electrode contact, sweating, and electrical interference.
Q12. Does EEG show the anatomical structure of the brain?
No. EEG records electrical function. CT and MRI are used primarily to assess brain structure.
Q13. Can EEG diagnose brain death by itself?
No. EEG alone cannot establish brain death. The determination must follow applicable clinical, legal, and institutional criteria; ancillary tests are used only where appropriate.
Q14. Why may sleep deprivation be requested before EEG?
Sleep deprivation may increase the likelihood of detecting epileptiform abnormalities in selected patients. It should be undertaken only according to the clinical team's instructions.
